theorem.statement:
Let \(K_{\!*}=\{k:|\mathcal S_k|>1\}\), and, for \(a\in\{0,1\}\) and \(c\in\mathcal C_{+}\), let \(\mathcal P_{a,c}=\{m\in\mathcal M:r_a(m\mid c)>0\}\).  At \(\Gamma=1\), the response-support family \(\mathcal P_{a,c}\) point identifies \(q_a(c,\cdot)\) for every compatible observed law if and only if it contains a pattern \(m^{\star}\) satisfying \(m^{\star}_k=1\) for every \(k\in K_{\!*}\).  In that case
\[
 q_a(c,s)=\frac{H_a(c,m^{\star},\operatorname{pr}_{m^{\star}}s)}{r_a(m^{\star}\mid c)}.
\]
Whenever this condition holds in every arm and positive-mass stratum, and also under complete response for every finite \(\Gamma\geq1\), the sharp endpoints have the following cut representation.  For \(Q\subseteq\mathcal S\times\mathcal S\), define
\[
 N_Q(A)=\{s_1\in\mathcal S:\exists s_0\in A\text{ with }(s_0,s_1)\in Q\},
 \qquad
 D_{Q,c}=\max_{A\subseteq\mathcal S}
 \left\{\sum_{s_0\in A}q_0(c,s_0)-\sum_{s_1\in N_Q(A)}q_1(c,s_1)\right\},
\]
and \(D_Q=\sum_{c\in\mathcal C_{+}}D_{Q,c}\).  Then
\[
 L_{\Gamma}=D_{R^{\mathrm c}},
 \qquad
 U_{\Gamma}=1-D_R.
\]
One maximum-flow/minimum-cut computation on the disjoint union of the stratumwise \(R\)-networks returns an upper-endpoint coupling and the maximizing cuts in \(D_R\); a second computation with \(R^{\mathrm c}\) returns a lower-endpoint coupling and the maximizing cuts in \(D_{R^{\mathrm c}}\).  Both networks have size polynomial in \(|\mathcal C_{+}||\mathcal S|\).  If \(H_a\) is rational, then in these response regimes the completions and both endpoint couplings are rational, and scaling by a common denominator gives integral flows, residual matchings, and zero-one cut certificates.

This direct network conclusion does not extend to all response-pattern families.  There is a compatible one-stratum law with \(d=3\), \(\mathcal S=\{0,1\}^3\), \(\Gamma=1\), and positive patterns \(100,010,001\) for which the natural completion-incidence block of \(\mathfrak H_R\) contains an odd-cycle minor of determinant of absolute value two and has a vertex that remains half-integral after scaling the observed masses by their least common denominator six.  Hence, independently of the chosen product order and of \(R\), this natural signed incidence system is neither a network matrix up to row and column permutations and sign changes nor a balanced-hypergraph incidence system, and it has no denominator-preserving integral-flow certificate.  This is a frontier for the natural incidence formulation; it does not exclude a problem-specific extended network or submodular-flow formulation with auxiliary variables.
theorem.proof_tex:
Fix \(a\in\{0,1\}\) and \(c\in\mathcal C_{+}\).  We first characterize uniform point identification at \(\Gamma=1\) by linear projection algebra.  Because \(c\in\mathcal C_{+}\), \(\kappa(c)>0\).  The sensitivity inequalities in \(\mathcal F_1(H)\) read
\[
 r_a(m\mid c)q_a(c,s)
 \leq \lambda_a(c,s,m)
 \leq r_a(m\mid c)q_a(c,s),
\]
so equality holds:
\[
 \lambda_a(c,s,m)=r_a(m\mid c)q_a(c,s).
 \tag{1}
\]
For \(m\in\mathcal P_{a,c}\), substitution of (1) into the observed-projection equations and division by the strictly positive number \(r_a(m\mid c)\) give
\[
 \sum_{s:\operatorname{pr}_m(s)=z_m}q_a(c,s)
 =\frac{H_a(c,m,z_m)}{r_a(m\mid c)}.
 \tag{2}
\]
No division is made for a zero-probability pattern; (1) instead forces its \(\lambda_a\)-coordinates to zero.

Let \(P_{a,c}\) be the zero-one matrix whose columns are indexed by \(s\in\mathcal S\), whose rows are indexed by \((m,z_m)\) with \(m\in\mathcal P_{a,c}\), and whose entry is
\[
 P_{a,c}[(m,z_m),s]
 =\mathbf 1\{\operatorname{pr}_m(s)=z_m\}.
\]
Equation (2) says that the observed law supplies \(P_{a,c}q_a(c,\cdot)\).  Thus \(q_a(c,\cdot)\) is uniquely determined for every compatible right-hand side whenever
\[
 \operatorname{rank}(P_{a,c})=|\mathcal S|.
 \tag{3}
\]
If \(m^{\star}\in\mathcal P_{a,c}\) observes every coordinate in \(K_{\!*}\), then \(\operatorname{pr}_{m^{\star}}\) is injective on \(\mathcal S\): omitted coordinates have singleton state spaces.  The rows of \(P_{a,c}\) belonging to \(m^{\star}\) therefore contain a permuted identity matrix.  Condition (3) follows, and (2) gives the displayed formula for \(q_a(c,s)\).  The denominator is positive by the definition of \(\mathcal P_{a,c}\).

Conversely, suppose that no pattern in \(\mathcal P_{a,c}\) observes every coordinate in \(K_{\!*}\).  For each \(k\in K_{\!*}\), choose two distinct levels \(u_k,v_k\in\mathcal S_k\) and define \(h_k(u_k)=1\), \(h_k(v_k)=-1\), and \(h_k(t)=0\) at every other level.  For \(k\notin K_{\!*}\), define \(h_k\equiv1\) on the singleton \(\mathcal S_k\).  Set
\[
 v(s)=\prod_{k=1}^d h_k(s_k).
\]
This vector is nonzero.  Every \(m\in\mathcal P_{a,c}\) omits some \(k(m)\in K_{\!*}\).  For each projected state \(z_m\), finite-product factorization yields
\[
 \sum_{s:\operatorname{pr}_m(s)=z_m}v(s)=0,
\]
because the factor obtained by summing over the omitted coordinate \(k(m)\) is
\(\sum_{t\in\mathcal S_{k(m)}}h_{k(m)}(t)=0\).  Hence
\[
 P_{a,c}v=0.
 \tag{4}
\]
Also \(\sum_sv(s)=0\), by the same factorization.  Let \(q^{\circ}(s)=\kappa(c)/|\mathcal S|\).  Since \(q^{\circ}(s)>0\) for every state and the state space is finite, there is \(t>0\) small enough that
\[
 q^{+}=q^{\circ}+tv\geq0,
 \qquad
 q^{-}=q^{\circ}-tv\geq0.
\]
They are distinct and both have total mass \(\kappa(c)\).  Choose any strictly positive probabilities \(\{r(m):m\in\mathcal P_{a,c}\}\) summing to one and define
\[
 H(c,m,z_m)=r(m)
 \sum_{s:\operatorname{pr}_m(s)=z_m}q^{\circ}(s).
 \tag{5}
\]
By (4), replacing \(q^{\circ}\) in (5) by either \(q^+\) or \(q^-\) does not change \(H\).  With
\[
 \lambda^{\pm}(c,s,m)=r(m)q^{\pm}(s),
\]
the projection equations, completion equations, and both \(\Gamma=1\) sensitivity inequalities hold.  Either completion can be coupled to any other-arm completion of mass \(\kappa(c)\), for example by the product coupling divided by \(\kappa(c)>0\).  Thus one compatible observed law has two distinct completions, proving failure of uniform point identification.  This establishes the claimed if-and-only-if characterization.  The construction also covers all finite product orders because it uses only the product support, not the order relation.

We next derive the endpoint formulas by a capacitated Hall/max-flow argument, using the already-proved finite-relation cut-capacity lemma.  In the \(\Gamma=1\) regime just characterized, (1) and the displayed formula uniquely determine both \(\lambda_a\) and \(q_a\).  Under complete response, the complete-response reduction gives the same fixed \(q_a\) for every finite \(\Gamma\geq1\), with all other completion coordinates forced.  In either regime, summing the completion and projection equations gives
\[
 \sum_{s\in\mathcal S}q_a(c,s)=\kappa(c),
 \qquad a\in\{0,1\}.
 \tag{6}
\]
For a fixed \(c\) and relation \(Q\subseteq\mathcal S\times\mathcal S\), apply the finite-relation cut-capacity lemma with
\[
 T=\mathcal S,
 \qquad \mu_0(s)=q_0(c,s),
 \qquad \mu_1(s)=q_1(c,s),
 \qquad w=\kappa(c).
\]
The equality of total masses required by that lemma is exactly (6).  It gives
\[
 \max_{\pi_c}\sum_{(s_0,s_1)\in Q}\pi_c(s_0,s_1)
 =\kappa(c)-D_{Q,c},
 \tag{7}
\]
where \(\pi_c\) ranges over all couplings of the two displayed stratum masses, and both the maximum and a maximizing set in the definition of \(D_{Q,c}\) are attained.

The coupling constraints in \(\mathcal F_{\Gamma}(H)\) do not mix response strata.  Therefore choosing an optimizer in (7) separately for every \(c\in\mathcal C_{+}\) gives a feasible global coupling, and every feasible global coupling restricts to one of the stratumwise couplings in (7).  Objectives consequently add across strata.  Since \(\kappa\) is the mass function of \(C_i\) under \(\mathbb P^{\star}\), zero-mass strata are omitted and
\[
 \sum_{c\in\mathcal C_{+}}\kappa(c)=1.
 \tag{8}
\]
Taking \(Q=R\) in (7), summing, and using (8) yields
\[
 U_{\Gamma}
 =\sum_c\{\kappa(c)-D_{R,c}\}
 =1-D_R.
 \tag{9}
\]
For every coupling, its \(R\)-mass plus its \(R^{\mathrm c}\)-mass is its total mass.  Taking \(Q=R^{\mathrm c}\) in (7) therefore yields
\[
 L_{\Gamma}
 =1-\sum_c\{\kappa(c)-D_{R^{\mathrm c},c}\}
 =D_{R^{\mathrm c}}.
 \tag{10}
\]
The joint observed-data sharpness theorem now identifies (9)--(10) with the sharp causal identified-set endpoints, rather than merely with an outer transport relaxation, and embeds each returned coupling and completion in a compatible cluster law.

For completeness, the two algorithms are explicit.  For each \(c\), create a source, a left copy and a right copy of \(\mathcal S\), and a sink.  Give the source-to-left arcs capacities \(q_0(c,s_0)\), the right-to-sink arcs capacities \(q_1(c,s_1)\), and the left-to-right arcs capacity \(\kappa(c)+1\) when \((s_0,s_1)\in Q\).  The finite-relation cut-capacity lemma proves that a maximum flow, its residual matching, and its residual-reachability cut return respectively a complete maximizing coupling and a set attaining \(D_{Q,c}\).  Run this construction on the disjoint union over \(c\) first with \(Q=R\) and then with \(Q=R^{\mathrm c}\).  These are the asserted two flow computations.  There are \(O(|\mathcal C_{+}||\mathcal S|)\) vertices and \(O(|\mathcal C_{+}||\mathcal S|^2)\) arcs, so standard finite maximum-flow algorithms run in polynomial time.

If \(H_a\) is rational, then \(\kappa(c)=\sum_{m,z_m}H_a(c,m,z_m)\) and every positive \(r_a(m\mid c)\) are rational.  At \(\Gamma=1\), the completion formula and (1) therefore make \(q_a\) and \(\lambda_a\) rational.  Under complete response, the complete-response reduction gives \(q_a=H_a\) and forced rational \(\lambda_a\).  Choose a common positive integer denominator for these finitely many masses.  The integral-augmentation and residual-matching part of the finite-relation cut-capacity lemma then makes the scaled endpoint couplings integral, while residual reachability gives zero-one cut indicators.  This proves the rational-certificate claim.

Finally, invoke the proved three-coordinate projection obstruction.  It supplies a compatible one-stratum \(\Gamma=1\) law with the three positive singleton-coordinate patterns \(100,010,001\) whose natural completion-incidence matrix contains
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1&1&0\\
 1&0&1\\
 0&1&1
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \left|\det\begin{pmatrix}
 1&1&0\\
 1&0&1\\
 0&1&1
 \end{pmatrix}\right|=2.
 \tag{11}
\]
That lemma also constructs a feasible completion vertex whose four positive coordinates become \(3/2\) after multiplication by the observed law's least common denominator six.  The completion block is a submatrix of the full natural signed incidence system \(\mathfrak H_R\), and it is formed before strict-dominance edges are added.  Thus changing the product order or \(R\) cannot remove (11).  Absolute determinants are invariant under row and column permutations and sign changes, so (11) rules out a directed network matrix representation of this natural system; the odd square submatrix with exactly two ones in every row and column also violates the defining balancedness condition.  The half-integral scaled vertex rules out the claimed denominator-preserving integral-flow property.  These facts disprove a universal natural-incidence network or balanced-hypergraph reduction.  Because they concern the displayed formulation rather than every possible auxiliary-variable extension, they do not imply the stronger and unproved assertion that no extended network or submodular-flow representation exists.
